query: For high-entropy alloys intended as intermediate materials in plasma-facing reactor components, what single intervention could improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the expected outcome compared with current intermediate-layer performance, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A single post-deposition subsolvus anneal that induces short-range chemical ordering (e.g., B2-type in bcc or L12-type in fcc HEAs) and modest grain coarsening in a refractory high-entropy alloy interlayer will increase its high-temperature thermal conductivity and effective heat-transfer across a W/HEA/Cu(stack) without compromising structural integrity relative to the as-deposited, chemically random state.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline, chemically random solid-solution high-entropy alloy interlayer (100–1000 µm thick) between a tungsten plasma-facing surface and a Cu-based heat sink; deposited by PVD or AM; bcc-dominant refractory HEA variant capable of ordering (e.g., contains Al to promote B2 domains), residual stresses present, fine grains (<500 nm), no deliberate long-range order.
generation.intervention: Single subsolvus anneal at 0.6–0.7 Tm (absolute, based on HEA solidus) for 1–4 hours in high vacuum or inert gas (≤10⁻⁵ mbar O2/H2O), followed by controlled cool (≤10 K/min) to promote short-range order (B2/L12) and limited grain growth (factor ~2–5 in grain size) without full recrystallization.
generation.conditions: Service: 500–900°C at the interlayer, cyclic surface heat flux 5–20 MW m⁻² with 1–5 min on/off periods, thermal gradients up to ~10⁴ K m⁻¹, vacuum; ion/neutron exposure up to ~1 dpa during the evaluation window. Pre- and post-anneal characterization and testing at 25°C and 600–800°C.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of short-range chemical order domains and/or fine ordered precipitates within the HEA matrix plus modest grain coarsening; reduced site/mass disorder at the electron mean free path scale and fewer grain boundaries per unit length.
generation.mechanism: Short-range ordering decreases electron scattering from chemical disorder, and modest grain growth reduces grain-boundary scattering; together these raise electronic thermal conductivity (dominant at high T in metallic HEAs). Concurrent order/precipitation strengthening and residual stress relaxation preserve or improve high-temperature yield/creep strength and resistance to thermal-cycling fatigue, preventing integrity loss despite lower boundary density.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-deposited interlayer, the annealed HEA will exhibit: (a) +25–40% increase in intrinsic thermal conductivity at 600–800°C; (b) +15–30% increase in effective thermal conductance of the W/HEA/Cu stack under 5–20 MW m⁻² heat flux; (c) ≤10–15% reduction in yield strength at 600°C (or no reduction if order strengthening dominates) and no increase in creep rate at 700–800°C at a given stress; (d) equal or lower crack density after 1000 thermal cycles between 200°C and 800°C.
generation.baseline: As-deposited, chemically random nanocrystalline HEA interlayer currently used as an intermediate layer (no induced ordering), evaluated under identical thermal and mechanical loading.
generation.boundary: Applies to HEA compositions that can develop SRO or partial ordering without forming brittle continuous intermetallic networks (e.g., Al-containing bcc RHEAs or fcc HEAs with ordering tendency), thickness 100–1000 µm, anneal temperatures below those that cause excessive interdiffusion at W/HEA/Cu interfaces. May not hold if: (i) irradiation dose is high enough to disorder the SRO (>~1–2 dpa during service), (ii) anneal triggers continuous brittle phase formation or porosity, or (iii) grain growth exceeds ~5–10× leading to embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of the thermal-conductivity increase depends on composition-specific ordering propensity and irradiation stability of SRO; the balance between order-strengthening and grain-growth softening may vary. At higher dpa, irradiation disordering could reduce the conductivity gain. No supplied prior evidence here constrains exact percentage gains.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare W/HEA/Cu mock-ups with identical HEA deposition. Split into control (as-deposited) and treatment (annealed as specified). Verify SRO via diffraction and atom probe/STEM. Measure (i) intrinsic HEA thermal conductivity by laser flash or TDTR at 600–800°C; (ii) effective stack thermal conductance under 10 MW m⁻² heat flux using calorimetry and IR thermography; (iii) 0.2% yield strength at 600°C and steady-state creep rate at 750°C; (iv) crack density and interfacial delamination after 1000 thermal cycles between 200°C and 800°C in vacuum. Optionally, repeat after ~1 dpa ion irradiation at 600–700°C.
measurements: HEA thermal diffusivity and specific heat (laser flash/DSC) → thermal conductivity
Stack thermal conductance under controlled heat flux (calculated from temperature drops)
XRD (order superlattice reflections), diffuse scattering, and atom probe/STEM for SRO/precipitates
Creep rate at 750–800°C under constant stress
Crack density and delamination area after 1000 thermal cycles (SEM/XCT)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if any of the following are observed for the annealed group relative to control: (1) intrinsic HEA thermal conductivity gain at 600–800°C is <10%; or (2) effective stack thermal conductance gain under 10 MW m⁻² is <10%; or (3) 600°C yield strength decreases by >15% or creep rate at 750–800°C increases by >20% at equal stress; or (4) crack density or delaminated area after 1000 thermal cycles is higher by >20%.
